title: Chemistry 11 — Chapter 1: The Isotope Shipment
description: A shipment of tracer isotopes just arrived for certification. Before anything goes into the lab inventory, you need to read the atomic data correctly — structure, ions, isotopes, and where each element sits on the table.

mika.name: Ms. Mika Tan
mika.description: Won't certify a shipment until every atom on the manifest checks out.

dev.name: Dev
dev.description: Knows the vocabulary but mixes up the numbers under pressure.

manifest.name: Isotope Manifest
manifest.description: Atomic number, mass number, and abundance data for every sample in the shipment.

periodic_table.name: Periodic Table Card
periodic_table.description: Groups, periods, and trend arrows at a glance.

elements.text: New tracer isotopes just came in. Before any of this touches the inventory, every atom on the manifest has to check out — protons, neutrons, electrons, all of it.
Isn't the number on the periodic table basically the whole atom?

options.text: "No — there are two different numbers per element, and they tell you different things. Let's read the manifest properly."
"Pretty much, one number should cover it."

elements.text: Atomic number is the number of protons — it's what makes an element that element. Mass number is protons plus neutrons combined. For a neutral atom, the number of electrons always equals the number of protons.
Take sodium-23: atomic number 11, mass number 23. That's 11 protons, 11 electrons, and 23 minus 11 leaves 12 neutrons.

config.question: The manifest lists potassium-39, atomic number 19. How many neutrons does this atom have?

options.text: 19 — same as the number of protons

config.prompt: Silicon has atomic number 14. In a neutral silicon atom, how many electrons are there? (just the number)

elements.text: Some of these samples are listed as ions, not neutral atoms. What changed?

Atoms gain or lose electrons to reach a stable outer shell — the octet rule. Metals tend to lose electrons and become positive cations; nonmetals tend to gain electrons and become negative anions. Noble gases already have a full shell, so they mostly do neither.
Magnesium has 2 valence electrons, so it loses both to form Mg2+. Chlorine has 7, so it gains 1 to form Cl-.

config.prompt: Sort each element by what it typically does to reach a stable octet.

config.question: Aluminum has 3 valence electrons. To reach a stable octet, it loses all 3. What is the charge of the resulting ion?
config.explanation: Losing 3 negatively charged electrons leaves the ion with a net charge of 3+.

elements.text: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons — same protons, different mass. The atomic mass on the periodic table is a weighted average across all naturally occurring isotopes, based on how abundant each one actually is.
Chlorine has two natural isotopes: Cl-35 at 75% abundance and Cl-37 at 25%. Average mass = (0.75 x 35.0) + (0.25 x 37.0) = 26.25 + 9.25 = 35.5 — which is exactly what the periodic table lists.

config.prompt: Boron has two isotopes: boron-10 (mass 10.0 u, 20% abundance) and boron-11 (mass 11.0 u, 80% abundance). Calculate boron's average atomic mass, to 1 decimal place.

config.question: Carbon-14 is a radioisotope used to date ancient artifacts. Compared to the common isotope Carbon-12, Carbon-14 has:

options.text: 2 more neutrons, the same number of protons
2 more protons, the same number of neutrons

config.explanation: Isotopes of the same element always share the same proton count (that's what makes it carbon); the mass difference comes entirely from extra neutrons.

elements.text: One more thing — the manifest flags a few samples by 'expected trend.' What does that mean?

Moving left to right across a period, nuclear charge increases while the electrons stay in the same shell, so atomic radius shrinks and ionization energy rises — it takes more energy to pull an electron away. Moving down a group, each row adds a new electron shell, so atoms get bigger and ionization energy drops.

config.prompt: Sort each property by how it changes moving left to right across a period.
Sodium (Na), aluminum (Al), and chlorine (Cl) are all in period 3. Order them from smallest to largest atomic radius.

elements.text: Every atom on this manifest checks out — structure, charge, isotope math, and trend. This shipment is certified.
It's certified, but a few of those numbers were shaky. Let's tighten that up before the next shipment.

elements.prompt: The manifest is signed off. What now?

options.text: Walk Dev through the difference between atomic number and mass number one more time, from scratch.
Sign off and move the shipment into inventory. Good enough for today.

elements.text: So atomic number is identity, mass number is weight, and everything else — ions, isotopes, trends — follows from just those two numbers. That's a lot simpler than I thought.

ending.title: Atomic Certifier
ending.description: Certified the entire isotope shipment from atomic structure through periodic trends, and taught Dev the core logic behind it.

ending.title: Shipment Signed Off
ending.description: The manifest is certified and the shipment is in inventory. The deeper trend-reading lesson can wait.
